top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The results of the individual studies are presented in figure 2. Children and adolescents with low adherence to the MedDiet had greater odds of developing MetS compared to those with medium to high adherence. The OR for this association was 2.18, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.45 to 3.28 ( p < 0.001). The inconsistency among the studies, as assessed by the I² statistic, was 64.15%.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: A sensitivity analysis was conducted by sequentially omitting one study at a time to assess the robustness of the overall effect estimate. The pooled ORs remained stable across all iterations, ranging from 1.91 to 2.43, and all remained statistically significant (p ≤ 0.001). These findings indicate that no single study unduly influenced the overall results, supporting the robustness of the association between low adherence to the MedDiet and higher odds of MetS in children and adolescents (figure 4). top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The effect size of each study was evaluated using the odds ratio (OR) and its 95% confidence interval (CI). All studies were included in the meta-­ analysis to assess the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. All analyses were conducted using Stata version 17.0 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA).

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: A total of eight cross-­ sectional studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. The PRISMA flow chart is shown in figure 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents has been a topic of increasing interest in recent years. Our study revealed that children and adolescents with lower MedDiet adherence had a greater risk of MetS than did those with higher adherence, providing important insights into the potential benefits of the MedDiet for MetS in children and adolescents. Specifically, higher adherence to the MedDiet was associated with lower odds of MetS, which includes a clustering of metabolic abnormalities such as abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, dyslipidaemia and impaired glucose metabolism. Overall, our meta-­ analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross-­ sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta-­ analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross-­ sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Figure 3 Funnel plot. (2021) | 1.91 [1.32, 2.75] | 0.001 | | 1.32 | 3.74 | | These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well-­ designed systematic review and meta-­ analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta-­ analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health-­ related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega-­ 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non-­ Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross-­ sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well-­ designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta-­ analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross-­ sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta-­ analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long-­ term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.section: Data Collection Process And Data Items
top_evidence.text: The following information was extracted from the included studies: (a) reference (year); (b) country; (c) characteristics of the subjects, including total sample size, sex ratio, age range and mean age; (d) type of questionnaire used; and (e) outcome information, including information on MetS and adherence to the MedDiet. All results from each study that were compatible with each outcome domain were included. In cases where missing information was identified in the published paper, the relevant authors of those studies were contacted directly to request the missing information.
